title: Typed tool calling + low-latency SDK: PRD draft
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a product requirements draft for two tightly-coupled capabilities on the Hosted API: (1) a small, low-latency SDK surface optimized for streaming-first flows, and (2) a typed tool-calling contract that enables safe, machine-checkable tool invocation with streaming partial results. The goal is to make tool-enabled streaming experiences ergonomically simple for engineers while preserving predictable latency and backward compatibility with existing generation endpoints.

Context / motivation:
- Customers are building chat assistants that (a) need immediate partial responses (TTFB) and (b) must call external tools (search, database, enterprise APIs) deterministically when the model requests them.
- Current hosted API patterns either stream plain text tokens (good for UX) or perform tool calls as separate synchronous operations (good for safety). Combining both with typed structured output introduces complexity in the API contract and SDK ergonomics.
- This PRD explores a single API contract and SDK ergonomics that support: incremental streaming of typed events (tokens, structured tool-call intents, tool-call results), recoverable reconnections, and graceful fallbacks for older clients.

High-level goals:
- API contract for typed tool calls that is machine-parseable and streamable.
- SDK surface that makes the common flows 1–2 lines of code (streaming render, tool handler registration, auto-acknowledgement).
- TTFB target: p50 < 150ms for small prompts on hosted tier; streaming chunks delivered within 30–50ms when tokens are available.
- Safe default: tool calls require explicit developer opt-in per route; payloads include schema and versioning metadata.
- Backwards-compatible: older SDKs can fall back to non-typed streaming or sync tool pattern.

Non-goals:
- Full orchestration of multi-step tool workflows (e.g., complex transaction coordination). That's a later phase (Optimize/Private teams to extend).
- Full client-side type generation for all languages in v1 — we will ship JS + Python helpers first.

Terminology:
- TypedEvent: a stream event carrying a typed envelope: {kind, schema_id?, payload}. Kinds: token, partial_text, tool_intent, tool_result, error, end_of_stream.
- ToolIntent: specification of an inferred tool action (tool_id, inputs, confidence, schema_id).
- ToolResult: the canonical result for a tool invocation (tool_id, status, output, meta).

API contract (REST + streaming semantics):
- POST /v1/sessions.generate (header: Accept: text/event-stream or application/json-stream)
  - Request body: {model, prompt, stream: true, tooling: {enabled: true, allowed_tools: ["search", "kb"], require_ack: true}, output_schema: "urn:redwood:v1/chat-response"}  
  - Response (streaming SSE / JSONL): sequence of TypedEvent JSON objects separated by newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) or SSE payloads.
  - Final event entry: end_of_stream with status/metadata including latency tokens, route info.

Example stream sequence (simplified NDJSON):
{ "kind": "token", "payload": "Hello ", "seq": 1 }
{ "kind": "token", "payload": "world", "seq": 2 }
{ "kind": "tool_intent", "payload": { "tool_id": "enterprise_search", "inputs": {"q": "pricing for plan X"}, "schema_id": "urn:redwood:tool:search:v1" }, "seq": 3 }
{ "kind": "tool_result", "payload": { "tool_id": "enterprise_search", "status": "ok", "output": {"top_result": "Pricing is $Y"} }, "seq": 4 }
{ "kind": "token", "payload": "Found pricing: ", "seq": 5 }
{ "kind": "end_of_stream", "payload": {"request_id": "r_12345", "latency_ms": 142}}

Tool-calling handshake and safety model:
- Tool intents are suggestive: the model emits a ToolIntent event. The SDK or server must enforce a policy: either auto-invoke allowed tool(s) (if configured) or pause and surface the intent to an application handler that returns an ack or deny.
- require_ack flag in request controls behavior:
  - require_ack: true -> server pauses streaming output at the ToolIntent until the client sends a ToolAck event (or deny). This preserves ordering and developer control.
  - require_ack: false -> server may auto-invoke allowed tools without waiting for an explicit ack (faster, but higher risk).
- Tool inputs must include schema_id. SDKs will provide schema validators to prevent obviously malformed calls.
- All tool invocation events are logged in route trace for replay / audits. Audit log includes model_version, schema_id, inputs hash (no plaintext caching unless customer consents).

Structured output and schemas:
- output_schema in request binds the top-level structure the model should produce. When present, the stream will include a final structured payload event (or partial structured events) that conform to that schema.
- Schema types supported v1: JSON Schema draft-07 subset (objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans) + named enums.
- Schema evolution: schemas are referenced by urn plus version (e.g., urn:redwood:schemas:chat-response:v2). The runtime validates final payload against declared schema and emits schema_validation errors as part of the stream if mismatch occurs.

SDK ergonomics (JS + Python priorities):
- Goals: minimal ceremony for typical flows (chat + tools) and explicit control for advanced flows.
- Suggested JS surface (sketch):
  const client = new Redwood({ apiKey });
  // register tool handlers once at app boot
  client.tools.register('enterprise_search', async (inputs) => { return searchService.query(inputs.q); });

  // streaming chat render with built-in tool ack handling
  const stream = await client.chat.stream({ model: 'rwd-chat-1', prompt, toolsAllowed: ['enterprise_search'], requireToolAck: true, outputSchema: 'urn:redwood:schemas:chat-response:v1' });
  stream.on('token', chunk => renderInUI(chunk));
  stream.on('tool_intent', async (intent) => {
    // SDK gives a simple helper to auto-acknowledge if registered handler exists
    const handler = client.tools.get(intent.tool_id);
    if (handler) {
      stream.ackTool(intent.id); // tell server to proceed
      const res = await handler(intent.payload.inputs);
      stream.sendToolResult({ tool_id: intent.tool_id, output: res });
    } else {
      stream.denyTool(intent.id); // deny and continue
    }
  });
  stream.on('end', (meta) => { console.log('done', meta) });

- Python surface will mirror these semantics (async iterator for tokens, callback registration for tool events).
- Error surfaces: SDK should expose typed errors: SchemaValidationError, ToolDeniedError, StreamInterruptedError, PartialResultError.

Backward compatibility and fallback:
- If client does not request typed streaming, server will continue to support legacy text-token streaming (unchanged).
- If server does not support typed tool-calls for a model, it emits a special warning event and clients should fall back to asking model to emit a text-based intent that app parses synchronously.

Operational concerns and observability:
- Logging: every tool_intent and tool_result should be emitted to the route traces with hashed inputs and tool_id for cost attribution and auditing.
- Metrics to track: streaming TTFB (p50/p90), time between tool_intent and tool_result, percent of sessions using require_ack true vs false, schema_validation_failure_rate, reconnect count per 1000 streams.
- Rate limits: tool invocations count toward route usage; SDKs should optionally batch tool calls when request patterns are high-frequency (configurable).

Testing and QA plan:
- Unit tests: NDJSON parser/serializer, schema validator, ack/deny handshake, reconnection resume using last-seen seq id.
- Integration: end-to-end test with a test tool service that simulates latency, error codes, streaming partial tool results.
- Load: synthetic streaming traffic at different token sizes to validate p50 TTFB target across hosted pools.

Rollout plan (hosted):
- Phase 0 — internal dogfood (1–2 weeks): JS + Python SDKs, internal tools registered, flaky network reconnection test.
- Phase 1 — limited external beta (canary clients listed in beta program, 1% traffic): soft launch with require_ack default on; close monitoring for schema mismatch and latency regressions. (2–4 weeks)
- Phase 2 — ramp to GA: expose as an opt-in route flag; docs published + migration guide for older SDKs. (2–6 weeks)

Migration notes for customers:
- If you currently use plain token streaming and want to adopt typed tool calls, recommended quick path: leave stream-mode unchanged, enable tooling:false initially, then opt-in tooling:true with require_ack:false to validate semantics without blocking UX, then switch to require_ack:true once your handlers validated.
- Provide code patterns for common frameworks (React streaming UI, backend microservices).

Back-of-envelope UX examples (latency tradeoffs):
- require_ack:true + registered handler -> extra RTT for ack but strong ordering guarantees. For local microservice handlers, this should be < 50ms.
- require_ack:false -> likely 30–80ms faster end-to-end in most cases but harder to audit if unexpected tools are invoked.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Do we require signed tool intents for cross-region tool calls? (security)
- Should the server buffer partial structured output and only validate at end_of_stream, or validate incrementally and emit schema_validation events? (tradeoff: early feedback vs cost)
- SDK API naming: stream.ackTool vs stream.confirmToolCall — pick concise but explicit naming after user tests.
- How to best support typed codegen for strongly-typed languages (TS, Java, Go) without exploding surface area? Consider a small optional codegen CLI in Optimize.

Appendix: small examples and edge cases
- Reconnect semantics: client reconnects with last_seq_id; server replays any unacknowledged events starting from last_seq_id+1. If a tool_intent was already acked and a tool_result posted, server will include tool_result; if tool_result not yet posted server will include tool_intent and mark it as maybe-duplicate so client can dedupe.
- Partial tool results: Tools that stream their own output (e.g., long search) can emit tool_result events with kind: tool_result_partial; client should pipe partials to UI.
- Privacy: tools handling PII must be marked in tool registry; server enforces no-logging for these tools unless customer enables it.

Appendix B: quick checklist for engineering handoff
- [ ] Define/implement TypedEvent JSON schema and version it.
- [ ] Implement server side NDJSON/SSE encoder/decoder and safety checks for ack/deny flows.
- [ ] SDK JS and Python: streaming iterator, callbacks, ack helpers.
- [ ] Add route-level feature flag and telemetry.
- [ ] Build integration harness with instrumented test tool service.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic: we prioritize small consistent surface area that supports most chat+tool flows. Expect follow-ups on richer orchestration and multi-tool transactions in later PRDs.
- Please comment on whether we should move to binary protobuf streams for perf in v2 (tradeoff: backwards compatibility, observability).

References and inspiration:
- Similar patterns: tool-calling RFCs from other providers, SSE/NDJSON streaming patterns, webhook ack patterns in payment processors.
- Internal: hosting telemetry patterns (confluence:HOSTED-1234), SRE recommendations for p50 TTFB targets.

END of draft
